vectors.prompt: What is the cosine similarity between (1,0,1)(1,0,1)(1,0,1) and (0,1,1)(0,1,1)(0,1,1)?
vectors.explanation: The dot product is 1 and both norms are 2\sqrt22​, so cos⁡=1/2\cos=1/2cos=1/2, an angle of 60°.

vectors.prompt: Two vectors have a dot product of 0. What does that mean?
vectors.explanation: A zero dot product means cos⁡θ=0\cos\theta=0cosθ=0, so the vectors are at 90° (unless one is zero, a special case of the same statement).
options: One of them is the zero vector

vectors.prompt: For unit-length embeddings, ranking neighbours by Euclidean distance gives the same order as ranking by cosine similarity.
vectors.explanation: For unit vectors ∥x−y∥2=2−2cos⁡(x,y)\|\mathbf x-\mathbf y\|^2=2-2\cos(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)∥x−y∥2=2−2cos(x,y), a decreasing function of cosine. That is why vector databases normalize embeddings.

vectors.prompt: What is ∥(3,−4)∥1\|(3,-4)\|_1∥(3,−4)∥1​?
vectors.explanation: The L1 norm sums absolute values: 3 + 4 = 7. The L2 norm would be 5.

matrices.explanation: Inner dimensions (784) must match and disappear; the result takes the outer dimensions.
options: 784×784784\times784784×784
32×25632\times25632×256
256×32256\times32256×32

matrices.prompt: How many parameters does a 784 → 256 → 10 network with biases have?
matrices.explanation: 784⋅256+256+256⋅10+10=203,530784\cdot256+256+256\cdot10+10=203{,}530784⋅256+256+256⋅10+10=203,530.

matrices.prompt: Which statements about a square matrix A\mathbf AA are equivalent to "A\mathbf AA is invertible"? (select all)
matrices.explanation: Invertibility, full rank, independent columns and nonzero determinant are all the same condition. Symmetry is unrelated.
options: det⁡A≠0\det\mathbf A\neq0detA=0
A\mathbf AA has full rank
A\mathbf AA is symmetric
The columns of A\mathbf AA are linearly independent

matrices.prompt: A⊤A\mathbf A^\top\mathbf AA⊤A is positive semi-definite for every matrix A\mathbf AA.
matrices.explanation: x⊤A⊤Ax=∥Ax∥2≥0\mathbf x^\top\mathbf A^\top\mathbf A\mathbf x=\|\mathbf A\mathbf x\|^2\ge0x⊤A⊤Ax=∥Ax∥2≥0.

eigen-svd.prompt: What are the eigenvalues of (2112)\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}(21​12​)?
eigen-svd.explanation: (2−λ)2−1=0(2-\lambda)^2-1=0(2−λ)2−1=0 gives λ=3\lambda=3λ=3 and λ=1\lambda=1λ=1.

eigen-svd.prompt: A 4096×40964096\times40964096×4096 matrix is replaced by a rank-16 factorization BA\mathbf B\mathbf ABA. How many parameters does the factorization have?
eigen-svd.explanation: 4096⋅16+16⋅4096=131,0724096\cdot16+16\cdot4096=131{,}0724096⋅16+16⋅4096=131,072, under 1% of the original 16.8 million. This is the LoRA idea.

eigen-svd.prompt: According to the Eckart–Young theorem, the best rank-kkk approximation of a matrix is obtained by…
eigen-svd.explanation: Truncating the SVD minimizes the Frobenius and spectral error among all rank-kkk matrices.
options: keeping the kkk largest entries
keeping the top kkk singular values and vectors of the SVD
keeping the first kkk rows
rounding every entry to kkk bits

eigen-svd.prompt: If the largest eigenvalue magnitude of a matrix is below 1, repeatedly multiplying a vector by it makes the vector…
eigen-svd.explanation: Ak=QΛkQ⊤\mathbf A^k=\mathbf Q\boldsymbol\Lambda^k\mathbf Q^\topAk=QΛkQ⊤ and ∣λ∣k→0|\lambda|^k\to0∣λ∣k→0. The same mechanism makes RNN gradients vanish.

calculus.prompt: Which direction gives the fastest decrease of fff at a point?
calculus.explanation: By Cauchy–Schwarz the directional derivative ∇f⊤u\nabla f^\top\mathbf u∇f⊤u is most negative for u\mathbf uu along −∇f-\nabla f−∇f. Gradient descent steps that way.
options: ∇f\nabla f∇f
−∇f-\nabla f−∇f
Any direction orthogonal to ∇f\nabla f∇f
The direction of the largest coordinate

calculus.prompt: What is σ′(0)\sigma'(0)σ′(0) for the sigmoid σ(z)=1/(1+e−z)\sigma(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})σ(z)=1/(1+e−z)?
calculus.explanation: σ′(z)=σ(z)(1−σ(z))\sigma'(z)=\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))σ′(z)=σ(z)(1−σ(z)) and σ(0)=0.5\sigma(0)=0.5σ(0)=0.5, so 0.5⋅0.5=0.250.5\cdot0.5=0.250.5⋅0.5=0.25, its maximum value.

calculus.prompt: For f(x,y)=x2yf(x,y)=x^2yf(x,y)=x2y, what is ∂f/∂x\partial f/\partial x∂f/∂x at (1,3)(1,3)(1,3)?
calculus.explanation: ∂f/∂x=2xy=2⋅1⋅3=6\partial f/\partial x=2xy=2\cdot1\cdot3=6∂f/∂x=2xy=2⋅1⋅3=6.

calculus.prompt: Keeping only the first-order Taylor term and stepping δ=−η∇f\boldsymbol\delta=-\eta\nabla fδ=−η∇f gives gradient descent; also using the Hessian gives…
calculus.explanation: Minimizing the quadratic approximation gives δ=−H−1∇f\boldsymbol\delta=-\mathbf H^{-1}\nabla fδ=−H−1∇f, Newton's step.

options: a\mathbf aa
a⊤x\mathbf a^\top\mathbf xa⊤x
x\mathbf xx
2a2\mathbf a2a

gx⊤\mathbf g\mathbf x^\topgx⊤
xg⊤\mathbf x\mathbf g^\topxg⊤

matrix-calculus.prompt: The gradient of log⁡∑jezj\log\sum_je^{z_j}log∑j​ezj​ with respect to z\mathbf zz is…
matrix-calculus.explanation: ∂/∂zk=ezk/∑jezj\partial/\partial z_k=e^{z_k}/\sum_je^{z_j}∂/∂zk​=ezk​/∑j​ezj​, which is exactly the softmax.
options: z\mathbf zz
eze^{\mathbf z}ez
softmax⁡(z)\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf z)softmax(z)

matrix-calculus.prompt: Why use a central difference (f(x+ϵ)−f(x−ϵ))/2ϵ(f(x+\epsilon)-f(x-\epsilon))/2\epsilon(f(x+ϵ)−f(x−ϵ))/2ϵ for gradient checking rather than a one-sided one?
matrix-calculus.explanation: The first-order error terms cancel, so the central difference is far more accurate at the same ϵ\epsilonϵ.
options: Its error shrinks like ϵ2\epsilon^2ϵ2 instead of ϵ\epsilonϵ

probability.prompt: For X∼Uniform(0,1)X\sim\text{Uniform}(0,1)X∼Uniform(0,1), what is E[X2]\mathbb E[X^2]E[X2]?
probability.explanation: ∫01x2dx=1/3\int_0^1x^2dx=1/3∫01​x2dx=1/3. Note that (E[X])2=1/4(\mathbb E[X])^2=1/4(E[X])2=1/4, so E[g(X)]≠g(E[X])\mathbb E[g(X)]\neq g(\mathbb E[X])E[g(X)]=g(E[X]).

probability.prompt: A continuous density can take values greater than 1.
probability.explanation: Only areas under the density are probabilities. A uniform density on [0, 0.5] equals 2 everywhere on that interval.

probability.prompt: Linearity of expectation E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y]\mathbb E[X+Y]=\mathbb E[X]+\mathbb E[Y]E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y] requires XXX and YYY to be independent.
probability.explanation: Linearity always holds. Independence is needed for E[XY]=E[X]E[Y]\mathbb E[XY]=\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y]E[XY]=E[X]E[Y] and for variances to add.

probability.prompt: Why do we minimize the average loss on a dataset instead of the expected risk directly?
probability.explanation: The empirical risk is a Monte Carlo estimate of the expected risk; mini-batches are an even smaller estimate.
options: The data distribution is unknown, so we estimate the expectation with a sample average

variance-joint.prompt: What is the variance of Uniform(0,1)\text{Uniform}(0,1)Uniform(0,1)?
variance-joint.explanation: E[X2]−E[X]2=1/3−1/4=1/12\mathbb E[X^2]-\mathbb E[X]^2=1/3-1/4=1/12E[X2]−E[X]2=1/3−1/4=1/12.

variance-joint.explanation: Variances add for independent variables and scaling by 1/n1/n1/n divides by n2n^2n2: nσ2/n2n\sigma^2/n^2nσ2/n2. Larger batches give less noisy gradients for this reason.

variance-joint.prompt: A correlation of 0 between two variables proves they are independent.
variance-joint.explanation: Correlation measures only linear dependence. Y=X2Y=X^2Y=X2 with symmetric XXX has zero correlation but is completely determined by XXX.

variance-joint.prompt: Under squared loss, which predictor minimizes the expected error?
variance-joint.explanation: Squared loss is minimized by the conditional mean; absolute loss by the conditional median.
options: The conditional mean E[Y∣x]\mathbb E[Y\mid\mathbf x]E[Y∣x]
The most frequent value of YYY
The overall mean of YYY

bayes.prompt: A disease has 1% prevalence; the test has 99% sensitivity and a 5% false-positive rate. What is P(disease∣+)P(\text{disease}\mid+)P(disease∣+) as a probability?
bayes.explanation: 0.99⋅0.01/(0.99⋅0.01+0.05⋅0.99)≈0.1670.99\cdot0.01/(0.99\cdot0.01+0.05\cdot0.99)\approx0.1670.99⋅0.01/(0.99⋅0.01+0.05⋅0.99)≈0.167. Low base rates dominate.

bayes.prompt: Prior Beta(2, 2); you observe 8 heads in 10 flips. What is the posterior mean?
bayes.explanation: The posterior is Beta(10, 4) with mean 10/14 ≈ 0.714, pulled from 0.8 toward 0.5 by the prior.

bayes.prompt: In Bayes' theorem, which term is the likelihood?
bayes.explanation: The likelihood says how probable the observed data is under parameters θ\thetaθ.
options: p(θ)p(\theta)p(θ)
p(D∣θ)p(\mathcal D\mid\theta)p(D∣θ)
p(θ∣D)p(\theta\mid\mathcal D)p(θ∣D)
p(D)p(\mathcal D)p(D)

bayes.prompt: Laplace (add-one) smoothing in Naive Bayes corresponds to which prior?
bayes.explanation: Adding α=1\alpha=1α=1 to every count is the posterior mean under a Dirichlet(1, …, 1) prior.
options: A uniform Beta/Dirichlet prior with one pseudo-count per outcome

distributions.prompt: Assuming Gaussian noise on regression targets leads to which loss?
distributions.explanation: The negative log of a Gaussian density is a constant plus a squared error.

distributions.prompt: Which distribution models a binary label?
distributions.explanation: A Bernoulli(p) variable is 1 with probability p and 0 otherwise; its negative log-likelihood is binary cross-entropy.

distributions.prompt: What are the mean and variance of a Poisson(4) variable? Enter the variance.
distributions.explanation: For a Poisson distribution the mean and variance both equal λ\lambdaλ.

distributions.prompt: Sampling x=μ+Lϵ\mathbf x=\boldsymbol\mu+\mathbf L\boldsymbol\epsilonx=μ+Lϵ with LL⊤=Σ\mathbf L\mathbf L^\top=\boldsymbol\SigmaLL⊤=Σ and ϵ∼N(0,I)\boldsymbol\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,\mathbf I)ϵ∼N(0,I) produces samples from…
distributions.explanation: Affine maps of Gaussians are Gaussian with covariance LIL⊤=Σ\mathbf L\mathbf I\mathbf L^\top=\boldsymbol\SigmaLIL⊤=Σ. This is the reparameterization trick.
options: N(μ,I)\mathcal N(\boldsymbol\mu,\mathbf I)N(μ,I)
N(μ,Σ)\mathcal N(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)N(μ,Σ)
N(0,Σ2)\mathcal N(0,\boldsymbol\Sigma^2)N(0,Σ2)

estimation.prompt: What is the maximum-likelihood estimate of a Bernoulli parameter after 7 successes in 20 trials?
estimation.explanation: p^=k/n=7/20\hat p=k/n=7/20p^​=k/n=7/20.

estimation.prompt: MAP estimation with a Gaussian prior on the weights is equivalent to adding which penalty?
estimation.explanation: −log⁡N(θ;0,τ2I)=∥θ∥2/2τ2+const-\log\mathcal N(\theta;0,\tau^2\mathbf I)=\|\theta\|^2/2\tau^2+\text{const}−logN(θ;0,τ2I)=∥θ∥2/2τ2+const.

estimation.prompt: A p-value of 0.03 means there is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true.
estimation.explanation: It is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null were true. It is not the probability of the null itself.

estimation.prompt: Dividing by nnn instead of n−1n-1n−1 when estimating variance gives an estimate that is…
estimation.explanation: E[σ^MLE2]=n−1nσ2\mathbb E[\hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}}]=\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2E[σ^MLE2​]=nn−1​σ2; Bessel's correction removes the bias.

info-theory.prompt: What is the entropy of a fair coin, in bits?
info-theory.explanation: −2⋅0.5log⁡20.5=1-2\cdot0.5\log_2 0.5=1−2⋅0.5log2​0.5=1 bit, the maximum for two outcomes.

info-theory.prompt: Minimizing cross-entropy H(p,q)H(p,q)H(p,q) over a model qqq is equivalent to… (select all)
info-theory.explanation: H(p,q)=H(p)+DKL(p∥q)H(p,q)=H(p)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)H(p,q)=H(p)+DKL​(p∥q) and H(p)H(p)H(p) is fixed by the data, so the three objectives coincide. KL is not symmetric, so the reverse KL is a different objective.
options: minimizing DKL(p∥q)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)DKL​(p∥q)
maximizing the entropy of qqq
minimizing DKL(q∥p)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)DKL​(q∥p)

info-theory.prompt: A language model has perplexity 20 on a test set. What does that mean?
info-theory.explanation: Perplexity is exp⁡(cross-entropy)\exp(\text{cross-entropy})exp(cross-entropy), the effective number of equally likely choices.
options: It is as uncertain as a uniform choice among about 20 tokens at each step

info-theory.prompt: KL divergence can be negative when qqq is a better model than ppp.
info-theory.explanation: By Gibbs' inequality DKL(p∥q)≥0D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\ge0DKL​(p∥q)≥0 always, with equality only when p=qp=qp=q.

optimization.prompt: For L(θ)=3θ2\mathcal L(\theta)=3\theta^2L(θ)=3θ2, what is the largest learning rate for which gradient descent converges? (Enter the bound.)
optimization.explanation: The curvature is L′′=6\mathcal L''=6L′′=6, and GD converges iff η<2/6\eta\lt2/6η<2/6.

optimization.prompt: Why does gradient descent struggle on ill-conditioned problems?
optimization.explanation: The slowest direction shrinks by roughly 1−1/κ1-1/\kappa1−1/κ per step, where κ\kappaκ is the condition number.
options: The learning rate must suit the steepest direction, so flat directions progress very slowly

optimization.prompt: Why does Adam apply bias correction to its moment estimates?
optimization.explanation: Dividing by 1−βt1-\beta^t1−βt removes the startup bias of the exponential moving averages.
options: The moments start at zero, so early averages are biased toward zero
To make it equivalent to SGD

optimization.prompt: Which are convex training objectives? (select all)
optimization.explanation: Linear models with these losses are convex. Neural networks are not, though gradient methods still train them well.
options: A two-layer neural network with cross-entropy
A linear SVM with hinge loss

optimization.prompt: What does a learning-rate warmup do?
optimization.explanation: Early on, Adam's statistics and the model are unstable; ramping the rate up avoids destructive first steps.
options: Starts with a large learning rate and decreases it
Increases the learning rate gradually over the first steps

numerics.prompt: Which format keeps fp32's exponent range but has far less precision?
numerics.explanation: bf16 has 8 exponent bits like fp32 and only 7 mantissa bits, so gradients rarely overflow or underflow.

numerics.prompt: Why is log⁡∑iezi\log\sum_ie^{z_i}log∑i​ezi​ computed as m+log⁡∑iezi−mm+\log\sum_ie^{z_i-m}m+log∑i​ezi​−m with m=max⁡izim=\max_iz_im=maxi​zi​?
numerics.explanation: Subtracting the max keeps every exponent at most 0, so nothing overflows, and the result is mathematically identical.
options: To avoid overflow when the ziz_izi​ are large
To make the result an integer
To change the result slightly for regularization

numerics.prompt: In fp32, 1+10−81+10^{-8}1+10−8 evaluates to exactly 1.
numerics.explanation: fp32 has about 7 significant digits (ϵ≈1.2×10−7\epsilon\approx1.2\times10^{-7}ϵ≈1.2×10−7), so the tiny term is lost: this is swamping.

numerics.prompt: What is the largest finite value representable in fp16?
numerics.explanation: fp16 has only 5 exponent bits; anything above 65,504 overflows to infinity, which is why fp16 training needs loss scaling.

monte-carlo.prompt: A Monte Carlo estimate from 10,000 samples has a standard error of 0.02. How many samples give a standard error of 0.005?
monte-carlo.explanation: The error scales as 1/N1/\sqrt N1/N​: a 4× smaller error needs 16× the samples.

monte-carlo.prompt: Why does Metropolis–Hastings work with an unnormalized density p~\tilde pp~​?
monte-carlo.explanation: The acceptance probability uses p~(x′)/p~(x)\tilde p(x')/\tilde p(x)p~​(x′)/p~​(x), so the unknown constant divides out.

monte-carlo.prompt: The reparameterization gradient estimator generally has lower variance than the score-function (REINFORCE) estimator.
monte-carlo.explanation: It differentiates through the sample path itself. The score-function estimator works for discrete variables but is much noisier.

__exam.prompt: Which identities connect statistics to common losses? (select all)
__exam.explanation: A Laplace prior gives the L1 penalty, not L2.
